hints: Notice this is an isomerisation with only one product, so every atom you start with must end up in urea. Think atom conservation.
Count the atoms in urea, $\text{CO(NH}_2\text{)}_2$, and remember ammonium is $\text{NH}_4^+$. What atoms must be left for the cyanate ion?
A neutral salt needs its charges to cancel, so use the +1 charge on ammonium to work out the charge the cyanate ion must carry.
walkthrough:
**Spot that atoms are conserved**

Think of this like rearranging Lego bricks. Ammonium cyanate turns into only urea, so both must contain exactly the same atoms in total.

$$\text{ammonium cyanate} \rightarrow \text{urea only}$$

**Count atoms in the product, urea**

Urea is $\text{CO(NH}_2\text{)}_2$. Count carefully and you get 1 C, 1 O, 2 N and 4 H.

$$\text{CO(NH}_2\text{)}_2 \text{ contains: C = 1, O = 1, N = 2, H = 4}$$

**Subtract what ammonium provides**

Ammonium ion is $\text{NH}_4^+$, so it supplies 1 N and 4 H. Take those away from the urea total to leave what the cyanate must supply.

$$\text{(C1 O1 N2 H4) - (N1 H4) = C1 O1 N1}$$

**Balance the charge**

Ammonium is +1, and the solid salt is neutral, so cyanate must be -1. That gives $\text{OCN}^-$ with the atoms C, O and one N.

options.A: Incorrect. $\text{CON}_2^-$ contains two nitrogens. Added to $\text{NH}_4^+$ this would give three nitrogens in total, but urea only has two. You have counted an extra N.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{CON}_2^{2-}$ has two errors. It has two nitrogens instead of one, and a 2- charge. With $\text{NH}_4^+$ it would neither balance atoms nor give a neutral salt.
options.C: Correct. $\text{OCN}^-$ has C1 O1 N1. Together with $\text{NH}_4^+$ this gives C1 O1 N2 H4, exactly the atoms in urea, and +1 with -1 gives a neutral compound.
options.D: Incorrect. $\text{OCN}^{2-}$ has the right atoms but the wrong charge. A 2- anion with $\text{NH}_4^+$ could not form a neutral 1:1 salt, you would need two ammoniums.
